exhibits.name: Apollo Lunar Module (descent stage)
exhibits.summary: The Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle had two stages. The ascent stage carried the astronauts back to orbit, while the descent stage stayed at the landing site for good, together with the EASEP science instruments.
exhibits.fact: The descent stage stayed at Tranquility Base. The ascent stage's final location is unknown; it is assumed to have crashed onto the Moon within one to four months.

signal.basis: Earth–Moon distance on that date, computed from a lunar ephemeris; light speed 299,792 km/s.

story: The Apollo 11 Lunar Module, named "Eagle" (LM-5), was the spacecraft that carried the first two astronauts to the surface of the Moon. Apollo 11 launched on July 16, 1969, from Cape Canaveral, Florida, aboard a Saturn V rocket. After reaching the Moon, Eagle separated from the Command and Service Module. Michael Collins stayed aboard it in lunar orbit, while Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin prepared to land.

On July 20, 1969, at 20:17:40 UT, Eagle landed in Mare Tranquillitatis, the Sea of Tranquility. Armstrong reported to mission control: "Houston, Tranquility Base here — the Eagle has landed." On July 21, 1969, at 02:56:15 UT, he stepped onto the surface and said his famous words, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." In the United States it was still the evening of July 20 because of the time difference. Aldrin followed about 19 minutes later.

Outside, the astronauts collected about 21.55 kilograms of lunar rocks and soil, took photographs, set up scientific experiments, placed an American flag, unveiled a plaque commemorating the first human landing and spoke with President Richard Nixon by radio telephone. They travelled about 250 meters in total, and moved as far as about 100 meters from the Lunar Module. Their time outside lasted about 2 hours and 15 minutes.

The Lunar Module was built in two parts. The lower part, the Descent Stage, helped the spacecraft land and served as the launching platform. The upper part, the Ascent Stage, held the crew compartment and carried the astronauts back to orbit. After about 21 hours and 36 minutes on the surface, Eagle lifted off on July 21, 1969, and the Ascent Stage docked with Collins aboard the Command and Service Module at 21:34:00 UT.

The two stages had different endings. The Descent Stage stayed at the Apollo 11 landing site after the astronauts left, and it did not return to Earth. The Ascent Stage was separated from the Command and Service Module at 00:01:01 UT on July 22. Its exact final location is unknown, and NASA's source states that it is assumed to have crashed onto the lunar surface sometime within the following one to four months.

The astronauts also left the EASEP scientific instruments on the Moon. Today the landing site is an important historical location, and the Descent Stage and other equipment left there are physical reminders of the first human landing on the Moon.

list: Name: Apollo 11 Lunar Module "Eagle"

Landing location: Mare Tranquillitatis (Sea of Tranquility), Moon

Mass: approximately 15,103 kilograms, including fuel and other propellants

details.title: General information
text: The Lunar Module was part of NASA's Apollo 11 mission, which made history in July 1969. It carried two astronauts, Neil Armstrong and Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin, who became the first humans to walk on the Moon.

The spacecraft also carried scientific equipment called EASEP (Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package). The astronauts placed this equipment on the lunar surface so it could collect scientific information after they left.

details.title: The first humans on the Moon
text: During their time outside the Lunar Module, the astronauts:
list: Collected lunar rocks and soil.
Took photographs of the lunar surface.
Set up scientific experiments.
Placed an American flag on the Moon.
Unveiled a plaque commemorating the first human landing.
Spoke with U.S. President Richard Nixon by radio telephone.
details.after: The astronauts collected approximately 21.55 kilograms of lunar rocks and soil. They travelled a total distance of about 250 meters on the lunar surface, and both moved as far as approximately 100 meters away from the Lunar Module. After completing their activities, they returned to Eagle. Their time outside the spacecraft lasted approximately 2 hours and 15 minutes.

details.title: How was the Lunar Module designed?
text: The Lunar Module was a special spacecraft designed to land on the Moon and return astronauts to the spacecraft waiting in lunar orbit. It had two main parts, called stages: the Descent Stage and the Ascent Stage. These two stages worked together during the landing and surface operations, but they had different jobs.

details.title: 1. The Descent Stage
text: The Descent Stage was the lower part of the Lunar Module. Its main job was to help the spacecraft land safely on the Moon. It had an octagonal shape and was approximately 4.2 meters wide and 1.7 meters thick. The stage included:
list: Four landing legs with round footpads.
A descent rocket engine.
Fuel and oxidizer tanks.
Water and oxygen tanks.
Storage space for scientific equipment and other supplies.
A small platform and ladder that allowed astronauts to reach the lunar surface.
details.after: The distance between the footpads of opposite landing legs was approximately 9.4 meters. The Descent Stage also served as a launching platform for the Ascent Stage. Important: the Descent Stage remained on the Moon after the astronauts left. It did not return to Earth.

details.title: 2. The Ascent Stage
text: The Ascent Stage was the upper part of the Lunar Module. It contained the astronauts' living and working area. Its main purpose was to take Armstrong and Aldrin from the Moon back to the Command and Service Module in lunar orbit. The stage was approximately 2.8 meters high and 4.0 by 4.3 meters wide. It included:
list: A pressurized crew compartment.
An entrance and exit hatch.
A docking hatch for connecting to the CSM.
Windows for observing the surroundings.
Control panels and navigation equipment.
Communication antennas.
An ascent rocket engine.
details.after: The crew compartment had a volume of approximately 6.65 cubic meters. Interestingly, there were no seats inside the Lunar Module. The astronauts operated the spacecraft while standing. After the astronauts finished their work on the Moon, the Ascent Stage lifted off from the Descent Stage and carried them back into lunar orbit.

details.title: How did the Lunar Module work?
text: The Lunar Module used rocket engines to control its movement and land on the Moon. Its two main engines had different purposes:
list: Descent Engine: helped the spacecraft slow down and land on the lunar surface. Its maximum thrust was approximately 45,000 newtons.
Ascent Engine: lifted the astronauts from the Moon and helped them return to the CSM. Its thrust was approximately 15,000 newtons.
details.after: The spacecraft also had a Reaction Control System, which used smaller rocket engines to control its direction and movement. Communication with Earth and the orbiting spacecraft was supported by radio antennas. The Lunar Module also had an environmental control system that supplied oxygen and controlled the temperature inside the cabin. Six silver-zinc batteries provided electrical power. For navigation, it used radar, gyroscopes, accelerometers, and the Apollo Guidance Computer.

details.title: EASEP: the scientific equipment left on the Moon
text: EASEP stands for Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package. It was a group of scientific instruments that Armstrong and Aldrin placed on the Moon during their mission. Its purpose was to collect information about the Moon and send scientific data back to Earth. EASEP was an early version of the larger scientific experiment packages used during later Apollo missions. The package had a total mass of approximately 48 kilograms. It included several important instruments:
list: Passive Seismometer: designed to measure seismic activity on the Moon. In simple words, it helped scientists study movements and vibrations inside the Moon. This information could help researchers understand the Moon's structure and interior.
Lunar Dust Detector: measured the accumulation of lunar dust and radiation damage to the solar cells. It helped scientists understand how the lunar environment affected equipment left on the surface.
Solar Panels: EASEP used two solar panels to collect energy from sunlight. The equipment could operate only during the lunar day because it depended on solar power.
Communication System: an antenna and communication system allowed EASEP to send scientific data to Earth and receive commands from ground stations.

Laser Ranging Retroreflector (LRRR): also considered part of the EASEP experiment package, although it was not physically attached to the main unit and did not require electrical power. It was placed approximately 5 meters north-northwest of EASEP. It was designed to reflect laser light sent from Earth, which allowed scientists to measure the distance between Earth and the Moon very accurately.

details.title: Where was EASEP placed?
text: The astronauts placed EASEP approximately 17 meters south of the Lunar Module. Its recorded coordinates were latitude 0.6735° N and longitude 23.4730° E.

The equipment was switched on by a command from Earth at 04:40:39 UT on July 21, 1969, while Armstrong and Aldrin were still on the lunar surface. It continued sending information to Earth until August 3, 1969, when its power began to decrease near lunar sunset. The equipment worked despite reaching temperatures approximately 30°C above its planned maximum operating temperature.
It was switched on again during the next lunar day. However, on August 27, 1969, it stopped accepting commands from Earth, and the experiment was ended.

details.title: What happened to the Lunar Module?
text: This is an important part of the Apollo 11 story because the Lunar Module had two separate stages. After spending approximately 21 hours and 36 minutes on the lunar surface, Eagle lifted off on July 21, 1969. The Ascent Stage carried Armstrong and Aldrin back into lunar orbit, where they met Michael Collins aboard the Command and Service Module. They docked at 21:34:00 UT.

After the astronauts transferred back to the CSM, the remaining Ascent Stage was separated from it at 00:01:01 UT on July 22. The exact final location of the Ascent Stage is unknown. The NASA source states that it is assumed to have crashed onto the lunar surface sometime within the following one to four months.
So, what actually remained on the Moon? There are two different parts to remember:
list: Descent Stage: stayed at the Apollo 11 landing site after the astronauts left.
Ascent Stage: carried the astronauts back to the CSM and was later separated from it in lunar orbit.
details.after: This distinction is important because the two stages had different purposes and different endings. The EASEP scientific instruments were also left on the lunar surface.

details.title: Why is Apollo 11 important?
text: Apollo 11 was one of the most important missions in the history of space exploration. It proved that humans could travel to the Moon, land there, work on its surface, and return safely.

The Lunar Module made this achievement possible by providing a vehicle designed specifically for landing on the Moon and launching astronauts back into lunar orbit. The scientific equipment left behind also helped researchers study the Moon after the astronauts had returned home.

Today, the Apollo 11 landing site is an important historical location. The Descent Stage and other equipment left there are physical reminders of the first human landing on the Moon. Apollo 11 was not only a successful space mission. It was a major step forward in human exploration beyond Earth.

details.title: Additional facts
list: The Lunar Module was also known as LM-5 and Eagle.
The landing site was in Mare Tranquillitatis, or the Sea of Tranquility.
The spacecraft had two stages with different purposes.
The astronauts collected 21.55 kilograms of lunar material.
EASEP had a total mass of 48 kilograms.
Armstrong and Aldrin travelled approximately 250 meters during their surface activities.
Michael Collins remained in lunar orbit while the other two astronauts explored the surface.

exhibits.name: Surveyor 3
exhibits.summary: One of the robotic Surveyor landers that proved soft landings on the Moon were possible. Two years later, Apollo 12 astronauts walked to it and brought home parts of the probe.
exhibits.fact: Apollo 12 landed a short walk from Surveyor 3, and the crew returned its camera to Earth for study.

signal.basis: Last contact May 4, 1967 (NASA Science). Distance computed from a lunar ephemeris.

story: Surveyor 3 was a robotic NASA lander sent to the Moon in 1967 to answer a simple question: is the lunar surface solid enough for astronauts to land on? It touched down in the Ocean of Storms on April 20, 1967.

Its landing was far from smooth. The main engine failed to switch off on time, and the lander bounced twice before it stopped. It then went to work, sending thousands of pictures and digging in the soil with a small scoop.
It stopped communicating on May 4, 1967. But the story did not end there: two and a half years later, Apollo 12 astronauts walked up to it, photographed it and took parts of it home.

details.title: Mission and scientific achievements
text: Surveyor 3 was one of NASA's robotic scouts for the Apollo program. Before sending people to the Moon, engineers needed to know how strong and how dusty the lunar soil was. Surveyor 3 carried two main tools to find out.
list: Television camera: it sent back 6,326 pictures of the lunar surface.
Surface sampler: a small scoop on an arm that could reach about 1.5 m (5 ft) from the lander and dig up to 18 cm (7 in) into the ground.
details.after: With the scoop the lander made 4 trenches, 4 bearing tests and 13 impact tests. In a bearing test the scoop is pressed into the soil to see how much weight it can carry; in an impact test the scoop is dropped on the soil to see how it reacts. Together these tests helped scientists understand the strength of lunar soil before the Apollo landings.

details.title: An unusual landing
text: Surveyor 3's main engine did not shut off at the planned moment. It kept firing until the lander was about 4.3 m (14 ft) above the ground, so the spacecraft hit the surface and bounced.
The first bounce reached about 10 m (33 ft) and the second about 3 m (10 ft). After the second one Surveyor 3 settled on the surface and kept working.

details.title: What happened to Surveyor 3?
text: Surveyor 3 stopped communicating with Earth on May 4, 1967. It stayed where it was, alone on the plain, for more than two years.

On November 19, 1969 (UTC), Apollo 12 astronauts Charles "Pete" Conrad Jr. and Alan L. Bean landed on the Moon about 180 m (590 ft) from Surveyor 3. During their second moonwalk they walked over to the old lander, photographed it, and removed several parts to take home:
list: its television camera system
the scoop of the surface sampler
sections of aluminum tubing
pieces of electrical cable
details.after: Back on Earth, NASA teams studied these parts for more than a year. By the time of the visit Surveyor 3 had spent about 31 months on the Moon, and engineers wanted to see how the lunar environment (strong sunlight, extreme temperatures, radiation, dust) had affected its materials, electronics and moving parts. The results were published in NASA's 1972 report on the Surveyor 3 material returned by Apollo 12.

images.alt: Apollo 12 astronaut at Surveyor 3, with the lunar module on the horizon
Apollo 12 astronaut beside Surveyor 3 on the Moon

facts.title: A spacecraft visited by astronauts
facts.text: More than two years after its landing, Surveyor 3 was visited by Apollo 12 astronauts, who recovered several of its components and brought them back to Earth.

facts.title: An unexpected landing
facts.text: Surveyor 3 bounced twice during landing because its engine did not shut down as planned.

facts.title: 6,326 pictures from the Moon
facts.text: The spacecraft transmitted 6,326 television images, helping scientists study the lunar surface.

importance: Surveyor 3 helped prepare for human exploration of the Moon. Its soil tests gave engineers real measurements of the lunar surface, which they needed before astronauts could land safely.

Its work continued even after its own mission ended. The parts recovered by Apollo 12 were a rare chance to inspect hardware that had spent more than two years on another world, and they taught engineers how spacecraft materials age in the lunar environment. A visit like this, to a spacecraft that had already ended its mission, is very rare in space exploration.

exhibits.name: Spirit & Opportunity (MER)
exhibits.summary: Two twin rovers landed on Mars in January 2004. They were planned for a few months of work and kept driving for years.
exhibits.fact: Spirit landed on Jan 3 and Opportunity on Jan 24, 2004 (Jan 4 and Jan 25 in UTC). Opportunity lost contact during a global dust storm.

signal.basis: Dates from NASA/JPL. Earth–Mars distance on each date computed from a planetary ephemeris.

story: Spirit and Opportunity were two almost identical robotic rovers built by NASA to explore Mars as part of the Mars Exploration Rover (MER) mission. Their main goal was to study rocks and soil and to look for evidence that liquid water once existed on the planet, so that scientists could understand what ancient Mars was like and whether it could have supported life billions of years ago.

Spirit was launched on June 10, 2003, and Opportunity followed on July 7. After about six months in space, each rover reached Mars inside its own spacecraft, slowed by a parachute and wrapped in airbags. Spirit landed on January 3, 2004, in Gusev Crater, where scientists thought a lake might once have existed. Opportunity landed on January 24, 2004, in Eagle Crater on Meridiani Planum, a region where orbiters had seen the mineral hematite, which on Earth can form in the presence of water.

Each rover was planned to work for 90 Martian days. Spirit worked for more than six years and discovered bright, silica-rich soil at a place called Home Plate. On Earth, such material forms around hot springs, so it suggested that Mars once had hot-spring environments. In 2009 Spirit became stuck in soft soil. NASA lost contact with it after March 22, 2010, and ended its recovery efforts on May 25, 2011, after it had travelled about 7.7 kilometers.

Opportunity worked for almost 15 years. It found small round hematite formations nicknamed "blueberries," the first meteorite ever found on another planet (Heat Shield Rock), and it studied craters such as Endurance, Victoria and Endeavour. In 2015 it became the first human-made vehicle to travel a marathon distance, 42.195 kilometers, on another world. By the end it had travelled about 45.16 kilometers.

In 2018 a massive dust storm covered a large part of Mars and blocked the sunlight that Opportunity's solar panels needed. Its last communication came on June 10, 2018, from Perseverance Valley, where it had just taken its final panorama. After many unsuccessful attempts to contact it, NASA declared the mission complete on February 13, 2019.

Together the two rovers showed that ancient Mars was not always the cold and dry planet we see today. It once had different environments involving water, including lakes, wet ground and possible hot springs. Their discoveries helped scientists plan later missions, including Curiosity and Perseverance.

details.title: Facts at a glance
list: Mission name: Mars Exploration Rover (MER)
Rovers: Spirit (MER-A) and Opportunity (MER-B)
Type: Robotic Mars rovers
Destination: Mars
Main objective: Search for evidence of ancient water
Launch period: June and July 2003
Landing period: January 2004
Original mission lifetime: 90 Martian days for each rover
Management: NASA and the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL)

details.title: Why did NASA send two rovers?
text: NASA wanted to study two different regions of Mars at the same time. Spirit and Opportunity were sent to opposite sides of the planet because scientists believed that both locations might have been affected by liquid water in the past.
Each rover had the same main scientific instruments, but they explored different environments and made different discoveries.

details.title: The journey to Mars
text: The two rovers travelled to Mars aboard separate spacecraft. Spirit was launched on June 10, 2003, from Cape Canaveral, Florida, aboard a Delta II rocket. Opportunity followed on July 7, 2003, using another Delta II rocket. Both spacecraft travelled for approximately six months before reaching Mars.

The rovers used a special landing system to reach the surface safely. First, a parachute slowed their descent through the Martian atmosphere. Then, large airbags inflated around the lander to protect it during landing.
After hitting the ground, the landers bounced several times before stopping. The airbags then deflated, allowing the rovers to open their landing platforms and begin exploring.

details.title: Spirit: the first rover
text: Spirit was the first of the two rovers to reach Mars. It landed on January 3, 2004, inside Gusev Crater. Scientists selected this location because they believed it might have once contained a lake. Its landing site was named Columbia Memorial Station in memory of the seven astronauts who died in the Space Shuttle Columbia accident in 2003.
list: Mission designation: MER-A
Launch date: June 10, 2003
Landing date: January 3, 2004
Landing location: Gusev Crater
Mass of rover: approximately 185 kilograms
Original mission duration: 90 Martian days
Last communication: March 22, 2010
Mission officially ended: May 25, 2011
Total distance travelled: approximately 7.7 kilometers

details.title: What did Spirit discover?
text: Spirit found strong evidence that ancient Mars was much wetter than it is today. One of its most important discoveries happened at a location called Home Plate. In 2007, Spirit's damaged front wheel dragged across the soil and uncovered bright material containing a very high amount of silica. Silica is a mineral commonly found in places such as hot springs and steam vents on Earth. This discovery suggested that water and possibly hot springs had existed in that area of Mars long ago.

Featured museum exhibit, Home Plate and silica-rich soil. What visitors can see: photographs of the bright soil uncovered by Spirit near Home Plate. Why it matters: the material contained a high amount of silica. On Earth, similar deposits can form around hot springs. This discovery provided evidence that ancient Mars may once have had hydrothermal environments.

Spirit also discovered rocks at a location called Comanche. These rocks contained large amounts of magnesium and iron carbonates. These minerals suggested that this area once had a warmer and wetter environment, with water that was less acidic than water found in some other locations explored by the rovers.

details.title: Problems and the end of Spirit's mission
text: In 2005, winds and dust devils sometimes cleaned dust from Spirit's solar panels. This allowed the rover to receive more sunlight and produce more electricity. However, the rover later experienced mechanical problems.

On May 1, 2009, Spirit became stuck in soft Martian soil. Its wheels could no longer get enough grip to move forward. One of its wheels had already stopped working, and another wheel later experienced a failure. NASA engineers tried many different ways to free the rover, but these attempts were unsuccessful.

In 2010, NASA changed Spirit's role. Instead of continuing to drive, it was planned to work as a stationary science platform. However, NASA stopped receiving signals from Spirit after March 22, 2010. Engineers continued trying to contact it, but they received no response. On May 25, 2011, NASA officially ended recovery efforts and declared the mission complete.
Spirit travelled approximately 7.7 kilometers and operated for more than six years. This was far beyond its original planned lifetime.

details.title: Opportunity: the long-distance explorer
text: Opportunity was Spirit's twin rover. It had almost the same design and scientific equipment, but it explored a completely different region of Mars. It landed on January 24, 2004, in a region called Meridiani Planum, inside a small impact crater known as Eagle Crater.

Scientists selected this area because observations from orbit showed signs of a mineral called hematite. On Earth, this mineral can form in environments involving water. Opportunity's landing site was later named Challenger Memorial Station, in memory of the Space Shuttle Challenger crew.
list: Mission designation: MER-B
Launch date: July 7, 2003
Landing date: January 24, 2004
Landing location: Meridiani Planum
Mass of rover: approximately 185 kilograms
Original mission duration: 90 Martian days
Last communication: June 10, 2018
Mission officially ended: February 13, 2019
Total distance travelled: approximately 45.16 kilometers

details.title: What did Opportunity discover?
text: One of Opportunity's most famous discoveries was the presence of small, round mineral formations on the Martian surface. These formations were made of a mineral called hematite and were nicknamed "blueberries" because of their round shape. Scientists studied them and found evidence that they had formed in an environment where water was present.
However, the water in this region was acidic. This means that although water existed there, the conditions may have been difficult for some forms of life.

Featured museum exhibit, Martian blueberries. What visitors can see: close-up photographs of the small, round hematite formations found by Opportunity. Why it matters: these formations provided evidence that liquid water had affected the rocks and soil in this region of Mars. Their shape and mineral composition helped scientists study the planet's ancient environment.

Opportunity also studied several large impact craters, including Eagle Crater, Endurance Crater, Victoria Crater, and Endeavour Crater. By examining the layers of rock and soil, it helped scientists understand how water, wind, and other geological processes had changed the Martian surface over time.

details.title: Heat Shield Rock: a meteorite on Mars
text: In January 2005, Opportunity discovered an unusual rock near its discarded heat shield. The rock was named Heat Shield Rock. Scientists examined it and found that it was an iron-nickel meteorite that had fallen onto the surface of Mars.

Featured museum exhibit, Heat Shield Rock. What visitors can see: images of Heat Shield Rock taken by Opportunity. Why it matters: it was the first meteorite discovered on another planet. Its composition showed that rocks from space can be found on the Martian surface.
Opportunity also studied a rock called Marquette Island, which appeared to have come from deep inside the Martian crust.

details.title: Opportunity's long journey
text: Opportunity travelled much farther than NASA originally expected. Its journey included several important locations:
list: Eagle Crater: its landing area, where it began studying Martian rocks and soil.
Endurance Crater: one of its early major exploration targets.
Victoria Crater: a large crater that the rover reached in September 2006.
Endeavour Crater: a much larger crater that Opportunity reached in August 2011.
Perseverance Valley: the region where the rover spent its final months.
details.after: In 2005, Opportunity became stuck in soft sand. Several of its wheels were buried, but NASA engineers managed to free it after approximately six weeks of careful work. The rover also survived major dust storms in 2007. These storms reduced the amount of sunlight reaching its solar panels, making it difficult to generate enough electricity. In 2015, Opportunity became the first human-made vehicle to travel a marathon distance on another world: 42.195 kilometers. By the end of its mission, it had travelled approximately 45.16 kilometers.

details.title: Opportunity's final panorama
text: Before Opportunity stopped communicating with Earth, it took a large panoramic series of photographs from its location in Perseverance Valley. The images were taken between May 13 and June 10, 2018. They were later combined into a wide view of the surrounding Martian landscape.

Featured museum exhibit, Opportunity's final panorama. What visitors can see: a panoramic view of Perseverance Valley, captured by Opportunity near the end of its mission. Why it matters: this was the final panorama created from Opportunity's images. It gives visitors a view of the place where the rover spent its last days on Mars.

details.title: The end of Opportunity's mission
text: Opportunity's mission lasted almost 15 years, far beyond its original 90-Martian-day plan. In 2018, a massive dust storm spread across Mars and covered a large part of the planet. The storm blocked sunlight from reaching Opportunity's solar panels. Since the rover depended on solar energy, it could no longer produce enough electricity to continue normal operations.

The last communication from Opportunity was received on June 10, 2018. NASA continued trying to contact the rover and restore communication. After many unsuccessful attempts, NASA officially declared the mission complete on February 13, 2019.
Opportunity had travelled approximately 45.16 kilometers and worked on Mars for more than 14 years. Its final location was in Perseverance Valley, near Endeavour Crater.

details.title: How were the rovers designed?
text: Spirit and Opportunity were about the size of a golf cart. Each rover weighed approximately 185 kilograms and had six wheels that allowed it to travel across the Martian surface. Their design included several important systems:
list: Body: the main structure of the rover. It protected important equipment, including computers and electronics.
Computers: the onboard computers processed information and helped control the rover's systems.
Cameras and sensors: the cameras allowed scientists to observe the Martian landscape, while other instruments collected scientific information about rocks, soil, and the environment.
Robotic arm: each rover had a robotic arm with several joints. It could move scientific instruments close to rocks and soil so that scientists could examine them.
Wheels: the six wheels allowed the rover to move across the Martian surface and explore different locations.
Solar panels and batteries: the rovers used solar panels to collect energy from sunlight and rechargeable batteries to store electrical power.
Communication antennas: the antennas allowed the rovers to send information and images to Earth and receive commands from mission controllers.

details.title: Scientific instruments
text: Spirit and Opportunity carried the same main scientific instruments. Each one had a special purpose.
list: 1. Panoramic Camera (Pancam): took detailed color photographs of the Martian landscape. It consisted of two cameras that worked together to create panoramic and three-dimensional views.
2. Navigation Cameras (Navcam): helped the rovers observe the terrain around them. They provided images that helped mission teams plan routes and understand the surrounding environment.

3. Microscopic Imager (MI): a small camera mounted at the end of the robotic arm. It took very close black-and-white pictures of rocks and soil, which helped scientists study small details that could not be seen clearly with ordinary cameras.

4. Miniature Thermal Emission Spectrometer (Mini-TES): studied infrared light, which is related to heat. Different minerals produce different patterns of infrared radiation, so by studying these patterns scientists could identify minerals in rocks and soil.
5. Mössbauer Spectrometer (MB): studied minerals containing iron. It helped scientists identify different iron-bearing minerals in Martian rocks and soil.

6. Alpha Particle X-Ray Spectrometer (APXS): studied the chemical elements found in rocks and soil. It helped scientists understand what materials made up the Martian surface and how water and other geological processes had changed it.

7. Rock Abrasion Tool (RAT): attached to the robotic arm. It used a small grinding wheel to remove dust and the weathered outer surface of rocks. This exposed fresh material underneath, allowing the other instruments to study the rock more accurately.

8. Magnet Array: each rover carried magnets. These collected magnetic dust particles from the Martian environment. Scientists studied the collected particles to learn more about the composition and history of Martian dust.

9. Calibration Targets: special reference objects used to check the accuracy of the instruments. One of them was a sundial mounted on the rover. It helped scientists adjust the colors and brightness of panoramic images so that they could better understand the appearance of the Martian landscape.

details.title: How did scientists control the rovers?
text: Spirit and Opportunity were controlled by teams on Earth. Scientists and engineers studied images and information sent by the rovers, planned their next movements, and sent commands back to Mars.

The rovers also had onboard computers and software that allowed them to perform certain tasks automatically. This made it possible for the rovers to work efficiently, even when communication with Earth was delayed.

details.title: Comparing Spirit and Opportunity
text: Although the rovers had almost identical designs, their missions had different results.
list: Spirit: landed in Gusev Crater. Discovered evidence of ancient water and possible hot spring environments. Found silica-rich soil and unusual minerals. Travelled approximately 7.7 kilometers. Became stuck in soft soil in 2009. Last communicated with Earth on March 22, 2010. Mission officially ended on May 25, 2011.

Opportunity: landed in Meridiani Planum. Discovered hematite formations nicknamed "blueberries." Found the iron-nickel meteorite Heat Shield Rock. Studied many impact craters and different rock formations. Travelled approximately 45.16 kilometers. Last communicated with Earth on June 10, 2018. Mission officially ended on February 13, 2019.

details.title: Five featured exhibits
text: The mission produced many photographs and discoveries that can be presented as individual exhibits in a virtual space museum. These five show different parts of the mission: scientific discoveries, unusual objects, the rovers themselves, and the final stage of exploration.
list: Exhibit 1, Spirit's Home Plate discovery. Object: silica-rich soil discovered by Spirit. Location: Home Plate, Gusev Crater. Importance: the discovery suggested that ancient Mars may have had hot springs or other hydrothermal environments. Suggested media: close-up photographs of the bright silica-rich soil and images of Spirit exploring Home Plate.

Exhibit 2, Opportunity's Martian blueberries. Object: small, round hematite formations. Location: Meridiani Planum. Importance: these formations provided evidence that water once affected the Martian surface. Suggested media: close-up images of the formations taken by Opportunity's cameras.

Exhibit 3, Heat Shield Rock. Object: an iron-nickel meteorite discovered by Opportunity. Location: near Opportunity's landing area. Importance: it was the first meteorite discovered on another planet. Suggested media: photographs of the meteorite and the rover's discarded heat shield.

Exhibit 4, Opportunity's final panorama. Object: a panoramic image created from photographs taken by Opportunity. Location: Perseverance Valley, near Endeavour Crater. Importance: it shows the landscape around the rover near the end of its mission and represents its final photographic work. Suggested media: NASA's final Opportunity panorama, which visitors can explore as a wide landscape image.

Exhibit 5, Spirit and Opportunity rover models. Object: three-dimensional models of the two Mars rovers. Importance: visitors can explore the design of the rovers and understand how their cameras, wheels, robotic arms, and other systems worked. Suggested media: NASA's 3D rover models, diagrams, and photographs of both vehicles.

details.title: Why are some NASA numbers different?
text: When reading different NASA pages, you may notice that some dates and measurements are not exactly the same. This does not always mean that the information is incorrect. Sometimes NASA uses different time zones or describes different measurements.
list: Different landing dates: Spirit's landing is listed as January 3, 2004, while Opportunity's landing is listed as January 24, 2004, on NASA's main mission page. Some detailed records also show January 4 for Spirit and January 25 for Opportunity. The reason is the difference between local Pacific time and Universal Time (UTC). The landings happened late in the local evening, so the UTC calendar date was already the next day.

Different distance measurements: NASA sometimes rounds the distances travelled by the rovers. Spirit: approximately 7.7 kilometers, with a more precise figure of about 7.73 kilometers. Opportunity: approximately 45.16 kilometers. These values describe the same achievements, but one version may use rounded numbers.

Planned mission vs. actual mission: both rovers were originally designed for missions lasting only 90 Martian days. However, they continued working for years. Spirit operated for more than six years, while Opportunity worked for almost 15 years. The original duration describes what NASA expected at the beginning. The longer durations describe what actually happened.

Rover mass vs. spacecraft mass: some NASA technical records list a mass of approximately 1,062 kilograms, while other descriptions state that each rover weighed about 185 kilograms. The 185-kilogram figure refers to the rover itself. A larger figure can refer to the spacecraft and its additional landing equipment. It should not be confused with the mass of the rover alone.

details.title: The legacy of Spirit and Opportunity
text: Spirit and Opportunity changed our understanding of Mars. Before their mission, scientists had evidence that water might once have existed on the planet. However, the two rovers provided important discoveries directly from the Martian surface.

They showed that ancient Mars had several different water-related environments, including acidic water, warmer and less acidic conditions, and possible hot springs. Their discoveries helped scientists plan later missions, including Curiosity and Perseverance. The experience gained from operating Spirit and Opportunity also helped engineers improve rover navigation, software, and mission planning.

Although both rovers stopped working many years ago, their scientific contributions continue to influence Mars exploration. They proved that robotic explorers could survive much longer than expected and travel much farther than originally planned.

details.title: NASA resources and official sources
text: NASA provides additional materials that allow visitors to explore the mission in more detail: 3D rover models, an interactive visualization of Opportunity's journey, Mars images (panoramas, close-ups of rocks, rover tracks and landing sites), Opportunity's final panorama of Perseverance Valley, and mission videos about the landings, discoveries and history of the two rovers.

exhibits.name: Ingenuity Mars Helicopter
exhibits.summary: The first aircraft to make a controlled, powered flight on another planet. After its rotor blades were damaged, it stayed on the surface.
exhibits.fact: The helicopter was built for a handful of test flights and completed dozens.
story: Ingenuity was a lightweight helicopter with specially designed rotor blades, and it did something no aircraft had ever done before: a powered, controlled flight on another planet.

NASA originally expected it to perform no more than five test flights within approximately 30 days. Instead, the little helicopter completed 72 flights over almost three years. The original technology demonstration was so successful that NASA extended its mission and gave it additional tasks.
Its flights were autonomous. Engineers on Earth planned the flights and sent commands, but Ingenuity used its onboard computer and sensors to control its movements during flight.

On January 18, 2024, Ingenuity completed its final flight. The helicopter experienced an unexpected problem and made an early landing, and NASA later received images showing damage to one or more rotor blades. The damage meant that Ingenuity could no longer fly, and on January 25, 2024 NASA officially announced the end of the mission.

Although its flights were over, Ingenuity had already achieved much more than originally planned. It remained on the Martian surface as a stationary artifact of space exploration. It was more than a small helicopter: it was a technology demonstration that helped make future aerial exploration of Mars possible.

details.title: How Ingenuity worked
text: To solve the problem of flying on Mars, engineers created a lightweight helicopter with specially designed rotor blades.

Ingenuity used solar energy to charge its rechargeable lithium-ion batteries. The stored energy powered its systems and provided enough energy for a planned flight of approximately 90 seconds per Martian day.
The helicopter also had cameras and sensors that helped it understand its position and movement.
Communication with Earth was supported through the Perseverance rover.

details.title: Technical specifications
list: Mass: 1.8 kilograms (3.97 pounds)
Rotor blade span: Approximately 1.2 meters
Power source: Solar panel and rechargeable lithium-ion batteries
Average power during flight: Approximately 350 watts
Battery type: Lithium-ion
Flight environment: Martian atmosphere, less than 1% as dense as Earth's atmosphere

details.title: Understanding the different NASA numbers
text: Some NASA materials show different numbers for Ingenuity's flight altitude and distance. This does not necessarily mean that the information is incorrect.
The reason is that NASA presents both the helicopter's technical specifications and its actual achievements. These numbers describe different things.
list: 1. Flight altitude: 5 meters vs. 24 meters. NASA lists approximately 5 meters as the helicopter's flight altitude in its technical specifications. This describes its planned operating capability. However, during the mission, Ingenuity reached a maximum recorded altitude of 24 meters. The 5-meter figure is a technical specification, while 24 meters is an actual mission achievement.

2. Flight distance: 300 meters vs. 17 kilometers. NASA lists up to 300 meters as the helicopter's flight range in its technical specifications. However, Ingenuity travelled approximately 17 kilometers during its entire mission. These numbers describe different measurements. The 300-meter figure refers to the listed range for an individual flight, while 17 kilometers represents the total distance from all 72 flights combined.

3. Five planned flights vs. 72 completed flights. NASA originally expected Ingenuity to perform no more than five test flights within approximately 30 days. Instead, the helicopter completed 72 flights over almost three years. This happened because the original technology demonstration was so successful that NASA extended its mission and gave it additional tasks.
details.after: In short, some numbers describe what Ingenuity was designed or expected to do, while others describe what it actually achieved.

details.title: Why is Ingenuity important?
text: Ingenuity changed the way scientists think about exploring other planets.
Before its mission, no aircraft had ever completed a powered and controlled flight on another planet. Ingenuity proved that small flying vehicles could operate in the Martian atmosphere.
Its success showed that future missions could use helicopters to explore areas that are difficult for rovers to reach.
It also provided engineers with important information about flight in a very thin atmosphere.
It proved that powered flight on Mars was possible and provided valuable information for future aircraft designs.

details.title: What comes next?
text: NASA's future Mars helicopter plans build on the experience gained from Ingenuity.
One of the projects mentioned by NASA is SkyFall, which aims to deliver a group of next-generation helicopters to Mars.
These helicopters are planned to help scout possible human landing sites and search for underground water ice.
This shows how Ingenuity's successful mission could influence the design of future space exploration vehicles.

exhibits.name: Sojourner (Mars Pathfinder)
exhibits.summary: The first rover on Mars. It rolled off the Pathfinder lander and drove across another planet for the first time.
exhibits.fact: Named after Sojourner Truth, the abolitionist and women's rights activist.

signal.basis: Final data transmission from Pathfinder Sep 27, 1997 (NASA). Earth–Mars distance computed from a planetary ephemeris.

story: Sojourner was the first rover ever delivered to Mars. This small six-wheeled robot rode to the planet on the Mars Pathfinder lander and rolled onto the surface in July 1997.
Pathfinder landed in Ares Vallis, an ancient flood plain. It did not use rockets all the way down: it was wrapped in airbags and bounced across the ground until it stopped.
Sojourner was planned to work for 7 days. It worked for 83. It proved that a rover could drive on Mars, and every Mars rover since then follows in its tracks.

details.title: The landing: bouncing on airbags
text: Pathfinder was the first U.S. spacecraft to land with airbags. It hit the surface at about 14 m/s (31 mph), bounced about 15 times, and came to rest about 1 km from where it first touched the ground. Afterwards the lander was named the Carl Sagan Memorial Station.
On the night of July 5 (late on the second Martian day, called sol 2) Sojourner rolled down the lander's ramp and started to explore.

details.title: What Sojourner did
text: Sojourner pressed its APXS instrument against rocks to measure which chemical elements they contain. Scientists gave the rocks nicknames, among them Barnacle Bill, Yogi and Scooby Doo.
The rover stayed close to its lander. On Sol 75 (September 18) it made its farthest trip: more than 12 m away, which NASA called a mission record.

details.title: What the mission returned
text: Altogether Pathfinder sent back about 2.3 billion bits of data, including more than 16,500 images from the lander and 550 images from the rover. The final data transmission arrived on September 27, 1997, and NASA ended the mission on March 10, 1998.

exhibits.name: Viking 1 Lander
exhibits.summary: The first successful US lander on Mars. It worked for years and remains exactly at its landing point.
exhibits.fact: The first picture ever taken from the surface of Mars was a photo of Viking 1's own footpad.

signal.basis: Viking Lander 1 final transmission Nov 11, 1982 (NASA Science). Earth–Mars distance computed from a planetary ephemeris.

story: Viking 1 was a two-part spacecraft: an orbiter that circled Mars and a lander that went down to the surface. On July 20, 1976 the lander touched down in Chryse Planitia and became the first fully successful U.S. landing on Mars.

Within minutes it sent the first photograph ever taken from the surface of Mars. Over the next years it photographed the landscape, studied the weather, analyzed the soil and ran experiments that looked for signs of life.
The lander kept working until November 11, 1982, when a faulty command from Earth interrupted communications. Contact was never regained.

details.title: Launch, journey and arrival
text: Viking 1 launched from Cape Canaveral on August 20, 1975 and entered orbit around Mars on June 19, 1976. The orbiter then spent weeks photographing possible landing sites.

Those pictures showed that the planned site in Chryse was rougher than expected, so the lander was sent to a safer spot on the western slopes of Chryse Planitia, about 28 km (17 mi) from the original target. It separated from the orbiter at 08:32 UT and touched down at 11:53 UT on July 20, 1976.

details.title: Two spacecraft in one
text: The orbiter carried a two-camera imaging system, an instrument that mapped water vapor in the atmosphere and an infrared instrument that mapped temperatures.

The lander carried two cameras, a weather station, a seismometer, an X-ray fluorescence spectrometer for soil chemistry, a gas chromatograph mass spectrometer (GCMS, which looks for chemical compounds), a biology laboratory and a robotic sampler arm.

details.title: The search for life: what was confirmed and what is interpretation
text: The biology laboratory ran three experiments on Martian soil: Gas Exchange, Labeled Release and Pyrolytic Release. Each tested for a different kind of possible life.
list: Confirmed: some early results looked like biological activity. In Labeled Release, adding a nutrient solution to the soil caused a quick release of gas, and NASA says the combined data could be read as a weak positive sign.

Confirmed: the GCMS, the main test for organic (carbon-based) compounds, found none above its detection limit, and the lander's roughly 5,000 pictures showed no biological objects. The soil also contained a lot of sulfur.

Interpretation: NASA concluded at the time that there was no evidence of life, and that the results were probably caused by unusual soil chemistry. Scientists still debate details. In 2008 Phoenix discovered perchlorate salt in Martian soil, which has kept the discussion about Viking's organic test alive.
details.after: The honest summary: Viking 1 did not find life, and it did not prove that Mars is lifeless.

details.title: The end of the mission
text: The orbiter shut down on August 7, 1980, when it ran out of the gas used to control its orientation (its 1,489th orbit).

The lander operated until November 11, 1982, when a faulty command sent from Earth interrupted communications. Attempts to regain contact failed. In January 1982 its landing site had been renamed the Thomas Mutch Memorial Station, after the leader of the lander imaging team.

Its orbiter also photographed Mars from above and helped choose the lander's safer landing site.

exhibits.name: Phoenix Mars Lander
exhibits.creators: University of Arizona, NASA JPL, Lockheed Martin Space
exhibits.summary: Phoenix dug into the Martian arctic soil and confirmed water ice just below the surface. It stopped working as the polar winter closed in.
exhibits.fact: A camera on a NASA orbiter photographed Phoenix hanging from its parachute, the first time one spacecraft imaged another landing on a planet.

signal.basis: Last signal Nov 2, 2008 (NASA JPL). Earth–Mars distance computed from a planetary ephemeris.

story: Phoenix landed in the far north of Mars on May 25, 2008. Its job was to dig into the arctic soil and find out whether the ice just below the surface could once have supported life. It did not find life.
It slowed down with a parachute and rockets, and landed on three legs. Its robotic arm dug into the ground and uncovered ice.
It was designed to work for three months. It worked for more than five, until the Sun sank too low for its solar panels. Its last signal arrived on November 2, 2008.

details.title: Why the Martian Arctic?
text: Water ice near the poles is the easiest water on Mars to reach. NASA wanted to know whether the ice and soil there could have supported microbes, and what the climate of the arctic is like. Phoenix was built to study whether the environment was habitable, not to look for living things directly.

details.title: The instruments and what they did
list: Robotic arm: it could dig about 0.5 m (20 in) down. A camera on the arm took close-ups of soil and ice before and after samples went into the scoop.
Wet chemistry laboratory (part of the MECA instrument): it mixed soil with water to measure acidity and dissolved salts.
Weather station with a lidar (a laser that looks up): it tracked dust, clouds and snow overhead.
Cameras: together they returned more than 25,000 images.

details.title: What Phoenix found
text: These results are confirmed in NASA's end-of-mission summary:
list: Water ice just below the surface, in at least two kinds of deposits.
Soil that is mildly alkaline, unlike what earlier missions had found.
Perchlorate, a salt that affects the properties of ice and soil.
Calcium carbonate, a marker of past liquid water.
Snow falling from clouds. The laser saw snow about 4 km (2.5 mi) above the lander; the snow vaporized before reaching the ground.
Small amounts of salts that could serve as nutrients for life.
details.after: Phoenix did not discover life on Mars, and nothing it measured proves that life ever existed there.

details.title: The photograph of Phoenix on its parachute
text: On May 25, 2008, NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter was already pointed at Phoenix's expected path to record its radio signals. Its HiRISE camera also took a very slanted (oblique) picture from about 310 km above the surface, and Phoenix hanging from its parachute was in it.

The parachute had opened only 46 seconds earlier at an altitude of about 12.6 km, and Phoenix was 2 minutes and 52 seconds from landing. The parachute was about 10 m wide; the lander appears as a bright dot below it. It was the first time one spacecraft had photographed another one during its descent onto a planet.
Looks can deceive: in the picture Phoenix seems to fall into a large crater, but it landed about 20 km away from it. The crater only appears behind the lander because of the camera angle.

links.label: See the picture: Phoenix Makes a Grand Entrance (PIA10698)

details.title: The end of the mission
text: As northern summer turned to autumn, the days got shorter, the sky got dustier and cloudier, and it got colder. Phoenix's solar panels no longer made enough power to charge its batteries. Its last signal came on November 2, 2008, and NASA declared the mission over on November 10, 2008.

exhibits.name: InSight Lander
exhibits.summary: InSight listened to the inside of Mars with a seismometer. When dust covered its solar panels, it ran out of power.
exhibits.fact: InSight was the first mission dedicated to studying the deep interior of Mars, and it listened to more than 1,300 marsquakes.

signal.basis: Last communication Dec 15, 2022 (NASA JPL). Earth–Mars distance computed from a planetary ephemeris.

story: InSight landed on Mars on November 26, 2018, on the flat plain of Elysium Planitia. Its goal was to study the inside of Mars: how thick its crust is, what its mantle is like and how big its core is.

It did this with a seismometer, an instrument that feels ground shaking, which it set on the ground with a robotic arm. It recorded 1,319 marsquakes. A second instrument, a digging heat probe called the mole, did not reach its planned depth.
Over time dust covered its solar panels and its power ran low. After two missed contacts in December 2022, NASA ended the mission.

details.title: Why study the inside of Mars?
text: Mars and Earth are both rocky planets, so measuring the inside of Mars helps scientists understand how rocky planets, including Earth, formed. InSight's name stands for Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy and Heat Transport, which are the three techniques it used.

details.title: Marsquakes: how InSight listened
text: A marsquake is a shaking of the ground on Mars, like an earthquake. When a quake happens, seismic waves travel through the planet, and the way they bend and bounce reveals what the inside is made of. InSight's seismometer, SEIS, was provided by France's space agency CNES.

InSight and its partners detected 1,319 marsquakes. Many came from a region called Cerberus Fossae, about 1,500 km from the lander. Wind noise hid quakes in winter, so most were found during calm evenings. Some waves also came from meteoroid impacts: the two largest craters found are over 100 m wide.

details.title: What scientists learned about the inside of Mars
list: Crust: its average thickness is 24 to 72 km, somewhat thinner than earlier estimates.
Core: it is about 3,600 to 3,700 km across, at the upper end of earlier estimates. Mars is just under 6,800 km across.
Mars is seismically active, and the data also revealed local weather and magnetic remnants in the crust.
details.after: Scientists are still studying InSight's data, and new papers keep appearing.

details.title: The mole that could not dig
text: The heat probe, called the mole, was a self-hammering spike made by Germany's DLR. It was meant to dig down to about 5 m (16 ft) and measure heat flowing out of Mars. It could not reach that depth. The soil was clumpy and did not give the mole enough friction to push against, so it could not hammer deeper.

Engineers tried many new ideas with the robotic arm, pinning the mole and pressing on it with the scoop. The mole's probe ended up buried about 40 cm (16 in) deep. After trying since February 2019, the team gave up in January 2021. The planned heat-flow measurement was not fully achieved, but the mole still returned data on the soil's physical and thermal properties.

details.title: Two tiny helpers: MarCO
text: Two small satellites called MarCO-A and MarCO-B launched with InSight. They were the first interplanetary CubeSats. They flew past Mars during InSight's landing and relayed its radio signals to Earth in near real time. MarCO-B also took a picture of Mars from about 7,600 km away.

details.title: The dust problem and the end
text: Dust slowly covered the solar panels and cut the lander's power. Engineers found they could scoop up soil with the arm and sprinkle it onto the panels on windy days so the falling grains swept some dust away. Even so, the seismometer was the last instrument left running.

InSight took its final selfie on April 24, 2022 (sol 1,211). After two missed contacts, NASA ended the mission, and the last communication had been on December 15, 2022. The lander is believed to be out of power, in what engineers call "dead bus".

specs: United States, with France, Germany and other partners
Solar panels span 6.0 m (19 ft 8 in); robotic arm 1.8 m (5 ft 11 in)
SEIS seismometer, HP3 heat probe (the mole), RISE radio experiment, wind and temperature sensors

facts.title: First dedicated to Mars's deep interior
facts.text: InSight was the first Mars mission dedicated to studying the planet's deep interior.

facts.title: First seismometer set on Mars
facts.text: It was the first to place a seismometer directly on the Martian surface, and the first to use a robotic arm to grasp instruments on another planet.

facts.title: A West Coast launch
facts.text: InSight was the first interplanetary launch from the U.S. West Coast, from Vandenberg.

facts.title: Twice as long as planned
facts.text: The mission lasted 1,446 sols, more than twice its planned duration.

facts.title: MarCO, the first deep-space CubeSats
facts.text: The two MarCO CubeSats were the first CubeSats sent to deep space.

importance: InSight gave the first direct look at the inside of another rocky planet since the Apollo-era seismometers on the Moon. Its measurements of Mars's crust, mantle and core help scientists test ideas about how rocky planets, including Earth, formed and changed.
It also taught engineers about digging into soil and working with dust on solar-powered missions, lessons for future landers.

exhibits.name: Pioneer 10
exhibits.summary: The first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt and study Jupiter up close. Today it drifts silently out of the Solar System.
exhibits.fact: It carries a gold plaque with a message for others; Carl Sagan and Frank Drake were among its authors.

signal.basis: NASA: the last signal came from 12.23 billion km and took 11 hours 20 minutes to reach Earth (science.nasa.gov/mission/pioneer-10).

story: Pioneer 10 was launched on March 2, 1972. It was the first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt, and the first to fly close to Jupiter, passing the giant planet in December 1973 and sending back the first close-up pictures.

Jupiter's gravity then threw the probe out of the Solar System. It is now one of the most distant human-made objects, heading roughly toward the red star Aldebaran in the constellation Taurus. It will need about two million years to get there.

The spacecraft carries a gold-colored plaque with a message for anyone who might find it, designed by Carl Sagan and Frank Drake, with drawings of a man and a woman, the Solar System and the location of the Sun.

NASA last received a very weak signal from Pioneer 10 on January 22, 2003. Its nuclear power source had faded, and the spacecraft could no longer send transmissions all the way home. It keeps moving in silence.

details.title: Facts at a glance
list: Agency: NASA Ames Research Center, built with TRW
Launch: March 2, 1972
Last contact: January 2003
Distance: more than 140 times the distance between the Earth and the Sun
One-way light time: about 19 to 20 hours

details.title: The plaque
text: The plaque shows the Solar System, the position of the Sun relative to pulsars, and a man and a woman. It is a message in a bottle, thrown into the cosmic ocean.

details.title: Why it matters
text: Pioneer 10 showed that a spacecraft could cross the asteroid belt safely and survive the strong radiation near Jupiter. That gave courage to the Voyager missions that followed.

details.title: This model
text: The 3D model of Pioneer 10 is still in development. The shape you see is a temporary placeholder.

exhibits.name: Dawn Spacecraft
exhibits.summary: Dawn studied Vesta and Ceres. When its fuel ran out, it was left in a safe orbit around Ceres.
exhibits.fact: The first spacecraft to orbit two different bodies in the main asteroid belt.

signal.basis: JPL Dawn Journal, Oct 19, 2018: Dawn was 3.58 AU from Earth, about one hour round trip. Contact ended Oct 31–Nov 1, 2018.

story: Dawn was launched in September 2007 to visit the two largest bodies in the main asteroid belt, Vesta and Ceres. It reached Vesta in 2011, and in 2015 it became the first spacecraft to orbit a dwarf planet when it arrived at Ceres.

It was the first spacecraft to orbit two different bodies beyond Earth in the main belt. Dawn did this thanks to an ion engine, which gives a very small push for a very long time and made the change of targets possible.

Over the years the spacecraft lost some of its reaction wheels, which kept it pointed in the right direction, and it came to depend on a single fuel, hydrazine. When it ran out, around the end of October 2018, Dawn could no longer aim its antenna at Earth or its solar panels at the Sun.

NASA declared the mission over on November 1, 2018. The engineers had put the spacecraft in an orbit that guarantees it will not crash for at least 20 years, and with more than 99 percent confidence for at least 50 years. It circles Ceres as a silent monument.

details.title: Facts at a glance
list: Agency: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), with Orbital Sciences
Launch: September 2007
Arrival at Ceres: March 2015
End of mission: November 1, 2018
Distance traveled over the whole mission: about 6.9 billion km (4.3 billion miles)

details.title: Why the orbit matters
text: Ceres may have conditions of interest for the chemistry behind life, so NASA follows strict planetary protection rules. The spacecraft must not hit the surface for a long time, in case another mission needs to visit a clean world.

details.title: What Dawn found
text: At Ceres, Dawn photographed the bright regions of Occator Crater and mountains such as Ahuna Mons, and gave scientists a detailed picture of a world that had been only a point of light before.

details.title: This model
text: The 3D model of Dawn is still in development. The shape you see is a temporary placeholder.
